answers.question: Whether a truly ultra-micro / WhatsApp-only tier priced below SAR60-75/month can achieve sustainable unit economics given payment processing + hosting + support costs
answers.answer: Direct evidence shows a sub-60 SAR/month price point already exists in the Saudi ZATCA-invoicing market: BizzSols prices a ZATCA Phase-2 compliant invoicing+inventory+accounting product at 49 SAR/month, and Bridge Bills at 52 SAR/month (promo), i.e. below the 60-75 SAR threshold — proving vendors are willing to sell at that price, though their internal profitability/unit economics are not disclosed (no margin data found). On the cost side: WhatsApp Business API costs are very low at micro scale — Meta gives the first 1,000 service conversations/month free, and utility/template messages cost only ~0.04 SAR each (per whautomate.com), so a WhatsApp-only support/notification channel is cheap for a handful of customers. Payment-processing costs for collecting the subscription fee itself would be non-trivial relative to a tiny subscription: Moyasar charges ~1.95-2.4% + 1 SAR per card transaction and Tap ~2.5-2.85% + 1 SAR — on a 60 SAR/month charge that is roughly 2.4-4.4 SAR (4-7% of revenue) per billing cycle, which is a real but not fatal drag if support/hosting stay near-zero (e.g. a lightweight cloud stack for very few users). No source directly discusses hosting or support cost breakdown for a solo-run product at this exact price tier, so the full unit-economics picture (after payment fees, hosting, and founder time) remains a reasoned estimate rather than a documented fact.

answers.question: Whether Zoho's free tier actually includes ZATCA Phase-2 compliance or only the paid Books tiers do
answers.answer: Zoho runs two relevant products: (1) Zoho Invoice — a separate, permanently free product whose own Saudi marketing page explicitly states it is 'Free VAT e-invoicing software for small businesses' and that ZATCA-required elements (QR codes, e-signatures, XML) 'can be generated right in Zoho Invoice' for free — i.e. this free product does claim ZATCA e-invoicing is included at no cost. (2) Zoho Books — the fuller accounting suite has a separate forever-free plan limited to businesses with annual revenue under SAR 200,000 and up to 1,000 invoices/year; Zoho's own help/community text repeatedly states 'ensure you are subscribed to the appropriate Zoho Books plan that supports this feature' for Phase-2 e-invoicing, which implies some Phase-2 integration capabilities may be gated to specific (possibly paid) plans, but no page found explicitly confirms or denies free-plan inclusion, and attempts to fetch Zoho's own pricing/help pages directly failed (proxy connection errors) after fetch budget was exhausted, so this could not be fully resolved. Net: Zoho Invoice (free, standalone) = ZATCA e-invoicing included per its own marketing; Zoho Books (free tier, revenue-capped) = ambiguous/unconfirmed whether Phase-2 integration is fully included or requires upgrade.

answers.question: Real churn/willingness of the smallest merchants to switch from a free/cheap incumbent to a new unbranded solo product
answers.answer: No direct study, survey, or review data was found measuring actual switching rates of Saudi micro-merchants between invoicing/accounting tools, and no evidence was found of merchants switching specifically toward an unbranded new solo product (a genuine gap — NO_RELIABLE_EVIDENCE_FOUND on that narrow point). However, indirect evidence points to concrete triggers that push small merchants to reconsider their tool: (a) Zoho Books' own free plan has a hard cap (revenue <SAR 200,000/year and ≤1,000 invoices/year) — once a growing micro-merchant crosses this, they must either upgrade or switch elsewhere, a natural churn/switch trigger; (b) Daftra's Basic plan caps at ~100 invoices and 100 clients/month, creating a similar forced decision point; (c) a search snippet reports a Wafeq complaint that the vendor removed bank-integration features from its cheaper starter plan and moved them to a plan '5x the price' without notice — the kind of incumbent bait-and-switch that classically opens the door to competitors (single-source, WEAK evidence, could not verify by direct fetch); (d) a broader Arabic article on why digital payment/tool adoption stalls among small Saudi merchants cites low transaction value, thin margins, and accumulated registration/device/service fees as reasons merchants resist paying for tools at all — suggesting the smallest merchants are highly price-sensitive and slow to adopt (or switch) unless the offer is free or near-free, and loyalty is driven more by cost/inertia than brand. Overall: real switching happens around concrete triggers (hitting a free-plan cap, a price hike, a feature removal) rather than spontaneous brand preference, but no hard number on churn rate or switch propensity exists in public sources.
